title: Reports
text:
Statistical analysis of oceanographic data (Black Sea – Danube area)

This project aimed to understand how environmental conditions influence species distribution. Using oceanographic data, I applied statistical analyses (normality tests, clustering, PCA, biodiversity indices) to identify spatial patterns. Results showed that nutrient-rich, silty environments near the Danube support higher biodiversity, while more distant sandy areas host different communities.The complete script is available below.
Skills acquired:

Statistical analysis (Shapiro test, data transformation)
Biodiversity indices (Shannon, Simpson, evenness)
Multivariate analysis (PCA, clustering)
Distance metrics (Bray-Curtis, Hellinger, Chord)
Data visualization (maps, dendrograms, PCA plots)
Ecological data interpretation (species–environment relationships)






#Statistical analysis of oceanographic data (Black Sea – Danube area)

#Sample of the code used in this analysis

## 1. Data Import
#The datasets used in this analysis include species data, environmental variables, #and station information. They are imported and cleaned before analysis.

Especes <- read_excel("~/Desktop/master oceano/M2/Maths/Marilaure/Exam janvier/Especes.xlsx")
View(Especes)
Especes <- Especes[-c(2, 3, 25, 26),]

FullData <- read_excel("~/Desktop/master oceano/M2/Maths/Marilaure/Exam janvier/FullData.xlsx")
View(FullData)
FullData <- FullData[-1, ]

data_spc <- read.table("~/Desktop/master oceano/M2/Maths/Marilaure/Exam janvier/BiomassDominantSpecies.txt", header=TRUE, sep="\t")
data_env <- read.table("~/Desktop/master oceano/M2/Maths/Marilaure/Exam janvier/EnvData.txt", header=TRUE, sep="\t")
data_station <- read.table("~/Desktop/master oceano/M2/Maths/Marilaure/Exam janvier/Stations.txt", header=TRUE, sep="\t")


## 2. Data Preprocessing
#Data were cleaned and formatted. Some rows were removed and variables were #converted to numeric format when necessary, while keeping spatial variables #unchanged.

exclude_cols <- c("Depth", "latitude", "longitude", "Station")

FullData[] <- lapply(FullData, function(x) {
  if (!any(names(x) %in% exclude_cols)) {
    as.numeric(x)
  } else {
    x
  }
})

Especes[] <- lapply(Especes, function(x) {
  if (!any(names(x) %in% exclude_cols)) {
    as.numeric(x)
  } else {
    x
  }
})


## 3. Normality Analysis of Environmental Variables
#The distribution of environmental descriptors was assessed using histograms and #Shapiro-Wilk tests. When necessary, transformations were considered to improve #normality.

hist(data_env$Porosity, main="Histogramme de la Porosité", xlab="Porosité", freq=FALSE, col="lightblue")
abline(v = c(mean(data_env$Porosity),median(data_env$Porosity)), col=c("green", "blue"), lty=c(2,2), lwd=c(3, 3))
shapiro.test(data_env$Porosity)

hist(data_env$Grain, main = "Histogramme du Grain", xlab= "Grain", freq = FALSE, col = "lightblue")
abline(v=c(mean(data_env$Grain), median(data_env$Grain)), col= c("green", "blue"), lty=c(2,2), lwd=c(3,3))
shapiro.test(data_env$Grain)


## 4. Biodiversity Indices
#Several biodiversity indices were calculated to describe species diversity at each #station:
#- Species richness (N0)
#- Shannon index (H)
#- Hill numbers (N1, N2)
#- Evenness indices (J, E1, E2)

N0 <- rowSums(data_spc > 0)
H <- diversity(data_spc)
N1 <- exp(H)
N2 <- diversity(data_spc, "inv")
J <- H/log(N0)
E1 <- N1/N0
E2 <- N2/N0

div1 <- data.frame(N0, H, N1, N2, E1, E2, J)
div1


## 5. Spatial Distribution of Biodiversity
#The spatial distribution of biodiversity indices was visualized using geographic #coordinates (latitude and longitude). Point size and color represent biodiversity #levels.

ggplot(biodiv_map, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, size = N1, color = N1)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +  
  geom_text(aes(label = Station), hjust = -0.3, vjust = -0.5, size = 4, color = "black") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(3, 10)) +  
  scale_color_gradient(low = "blue", high = "gold") +  
  theme_minimal()
  
  
## 6. Distance Matrices
#Distance matrices between sites were computed using different metrics:
#- Bray-Curtis distance
#- Chord distance
#- Hellinger distance
#These metrics allow comparison of sites based on species composition and #environmental variables.

spe.db <- vegdist(d.spe)
spe.dbL <- vegdist(decostand(d.spe,'log'))
spe.dc <- dist(decostand(d.spe,'norm'))
spe.dh <- dist(decostand(d.spe,'hel'))

coldiss(spe.db)
coldiss(spe.dbL)
coldiss(spe.dc)
coldiss(spe.dh)


## 7. Cluster Analysis
#Hierarchical clustering was performed to group sites based on similarity. Several #clustering methods were compared:
#- Single linkage
#- Complete linkage
#- Average linkage (UPGMA)
#- Ward method
#The best method was selected using cophenetic correlation and silhouette analysis.

spe.norm2 <- decostand(d.spe2,'norm')
spe.dist2 <- dist(spe.norm2)

spe.dist.average2  <- hclust(spe.dist2, method= "average")
plot(spe.dist.average2)


## 8. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) – Species Data
#A PCA was performed on species data to identify patterns in species distribution #across stations.

spe.pca <- rda(spe.hel)
summary(spe.pca)

biplot(spe.pca, scaling=1)
biplot(spe.pca, scaling=2)


## 9. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) – Environmental Variables
#A PCA was conducted on environmental variables to identify major environmental #gradients influencing the system.

env.pca <- rda(d.env.sc)
summary(env.pca)

biplot(env.pca, scaling=1)
biplot(env.pca, scaling=2)


## 10. PCA on Biodiversity Indices
#A PCA was performed on biodiversity indices to explore relationships between #diversity metrics and identify patterns among stations.

env.pca <- rda(d.bio.valid)
summary(env.pca)

biplot(env.pca, scaling=1)
biplot(env.pca, scaling=2)

Internship in Stable Isotope Analysis

This internship focused on the ecophysiology of the Antarctic sea star Odontaster validus through stable isotope analysis. I was responsible for preparing biological samples (grinding, acidification, and encapsulation) to ensure accurate isotopic measurements. I also gained insight into isotopic techniques and the functioning of EA-IRMS instrumentation. This experience strengthened my laboratory skills, scientific rigor, and understanding of trophic ecology in marine ecosystems.
Skills acquired:

Sample preparation for stable isotope analysis (grinding, acidification, encapsulation)
Handling of laboratory equipment and chemical safety procedures
Understanding of stable isotope ecology (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N, δ³⁴S)
Knowledge of isotopic fractionation and tissue turnover concepts
Familiarity with EA-IRMS instrumentation and analytical workflow

It highlights key issues such as overfishing, disease outbreaks in aquaculture, and global competition, while proposing strategies for a more sustainable and quality-oriented development of the sector.

The Hidden Side of Oil Spills

Oil spills represent massive releases of hydrocarbons into the marine environment, with ecological impacts depending on the chemical composition of the oil, the affected ecosystem, and local physicochemical conditions. Hydrocarbons, particularly PAHs, can disperse, sediment, or bioaccumulate, affecting marine life from phytoplankton to mammals. Chemical dispersants accelerate oil fragmentation but may increase its toxicity to organisms. International regulations and local measures (sorbents, barriers, animal care) help mitigate impacts, yet risk assessment remains complex. Prevention and management of oil spills require a thorough understanding of hydrocarbon chemistry, marine ecology, and remediation techniques.
Skills acquired:

Environmental Chemistry & Toxicology (hydrocarbon composition, behavior, toxicity, including PAHs)
Marine Ecology & Ecosystem Impact Analysis
Pollution Mitigation & Remediation Techniques (dispersants, sorbents, skimmers, and cleanup strategies)
Regulatory & Risk Assessment Skills (international conventions, local regulations and environmental risk evaluation)
Scientific Research & Communication

Biochemistry and Physiology of Marine Animals (Collaborative Project)

This academic project explores the biochemistry and physiology of marine animals, focusing on the adaptations of blue-ringed octopuses (genus Hapalochlaena). It examines their evolutionary origins, habitat distribution, feeding strategies, reproductive behavior, and advanced camouflage systems. Particular attention is given to their unique use of tetrodotoxin (TTX), a powerful neurotoxin used for both predation and defense. This work highlights how morphological, physiological, and behavioral traits are finely tuned to environmental constraints.
Skills acquired:

Scientific research and literature review
Data synthesis and critical analysis
Academic writing in English
Team collaboration
Marine biology and biochemistry knowledge
Oral and written scientific communication

title: Master’s Thesis in Marine Biology
text:
Investigating the molecular mechanisms involved in the control and perception of bioluminescence in Tomopteris helgolandica


Summary

Bioluminescence is a widespread phenomenon in marine organisms, yet its molecular regulation remains poorly understood in many species. This study investigates the potential mechanisms involved in the control and perception of light emission in the polychaete Tomopteris helgolandica.
Previous transcriptomic analyses suggested the presence of opsin 4, an extraocular photoreceptor potentially involved in light perception. This work aimed to determine whether the molecular components involved in both light emission control and photoreception are present in this species. The study focused on two key elements: the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors potentially involved in the control of bioluminescence, and opsin 4, which may enable the organism to detect light signals.
Through transcriptomic and immunological approaches, this work explored the presence and localization of these proteins within the organism, providing insights into the potential coupling between light production and light perception in luminous marine organisms.


Keywords
Bioluminescence • Tomopteris helgolandica • opsin 4 • acetylcholine receptors • photoreception • marine polychaetes


Methods

Specimen collection and fixation of Tomopteris helgolandica
Transcriptomic analyses to identify genes involved in light emission and photoreception
In silico sequence analyses to detect opsin 4 and nicotinic acetylcholine receptor sequences
Phylogenetic analysis of identified sequences
Protein detection using Western blot
Immunohistological analyses to determine the localization of opsin 4 and acetylcholine receptors
Fluorescence microscopy to visualize protein expression in tissues




Key Results


Transcriptomic analyses revealed the presence of proteins involved in the signal transduction pathways of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and opsin 4.














Immunological analyses confirmed the presence and localization of these proteins in the rosette glands located in the parapodia of T. helgolandica.




These findings suggest that the species possesses the molecular components required both to control and to perceive its own bioluminescence.
The results provide the first evidence of a potential coupling between light emission and light perception in a polychaete species.
This mechanism may indicate a functional convergence in luminous organisms, where photoreception directly regulates light production at the emission site.

title: Master’s Thesis in oceanography
text:
Evaluating the spatio-temporal dynamics of low- and mid-trophic level resources in the Azores: implications for the new MPA network and cetacean populations

Summary

This study investigated the spatio-temporal distribution of low- and mid-trophic level biomass in the Azores using the SEPODYM-LMTL ecological model from 1998 to 2023. Three variables were analyzed: net primary production (NPP), zooplankton, and micronekton. Areas were classified into three productivity zones: recurrent, occasional, and unfavorable. Productivity within the new Marine Protected Area (MPA) network was assessed to see if MPAs overlapped with highly productive waters.
Inter-annual variability was high, with no overall trends in NPP or zooplankton biomass. Spatial distribution showed a strong latitudinal gradient, with high productivity near the islands and north of 37°N (Azores Counter Current). Fully protected MPAs had higher productivity from April to November, while highly protected areas were similar or lower than unprotected zones.
Baleen whales were mostly observed in occasional productivity zones, particularly in July; no clear patterns emerged for dolphins or deep-diving species. These results provide a baseline for evaluating the ecological value of MPAs and suggest productivity zones may be important for higher trophic levels. Long-term monitoring and additional environmental predictors are needed to fully understand their significance.


Keywords
 SEAPODYM-LMTL • trophic levels • productivity zones • marine protected areas • cetaceans 


Methods
 - Ecological model outputs from SEAPODYM-LMTL - Analysis of three productivity indicators - Net Primary Production (NPP)
- Zooplankton biomass
- Micronekton biomass - Time series analysis (1998–2023) - Spatial analysis of productivity hotspots - Classification of productivity zones - recurrent
- occasional
- unfavorable - Comparison with Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) - Cetacean sightings dataset from the POPA program (2001–2015) 



Key Results

 - Strong spatial heterogeneity in marine productivity across the Azores. 



 - A high-productivity region was identified around the islands and north of 37°N. 



 - Fully protected MPAs tend to overlap with more productive waters, especially between April and November. 



 - Baleen whales were more frequently observed in occasional productivity zones, particularly during summer. - No clear association was detected for dolphins and deep-diving cetaceans.

📧 annenoe.vanhove@outlook.fr




I am a marine biologist studying ecosystem dynamics, trophic interactions, and ecological modeling in marine systems.





My academic background spans multiple scales, from cellular biology and organism physiology to ecosystem dynamics. I first trained in small-scale biological processes before pursuing two Master’s degrees: one in organismal biology and ecology focused on conservation and restoration, and another in oceanography, including physical and chemical processes, trophic interactions, and large-scale ecosystem dynamics. This training allows me to approach marine ecosystems as integrated systems across scales, from fine-scale processes to large-scale dynamics.
This portfolio presents my research projects, including my master’s thesis and other academic work.
